It builds on the round-one files 04_neuro_death_eyes.md and 01_gunshot_wounds.md without repeating them. Every section ends with a "Simulation parameters" table and a "Visual/behavioural checklist". About 115 web searches were run until the shared search budget ran out. WebFetch was blocked, so every [S#] value comes from search-result summaries, and a QA list of what to check first is in §21. Key findings:

1. Side rules. Cortex, internal capsule, basal ganglia, thalamus and cerebral peduncle affect the opposite side of the body. The cerebellum affects the same side. A brainstem lesion gives crossed signs: eye, face and tongue problems on the wound side, limb weakness on the other side [K][S47][S53][S60].

2. Motor cortex. The homunculus is mapped to a coordinate s along the strip. The hand knob lies about 35 mm from the midline and 15–20 mm deep [S34]. Wrist MNI coordinates are (27, −25, 70) [S35]. The lower face is weakened while the forehead is spared [S36]. Paralysis is limp from the first moment. Spasticity appears after 1–6 weeks, in 24.5% by 2 weeks and 39.5% overall [S1][S2]. So within game time a brain-damaged limb is always limp.

3. Internal capsule. A deep lesion of 2–20 mm gives a dense one-sided paralysis of face, arm and leg equally [S31]. Game mapping: visible at 0.05, full at 0.30 of the region destroyed [E].

4. Frontal regions.
   - SMA damage gives akinesia with preserved strength, and mutism if left-sided. Speech recovers first, then leg, then arm; about 90% recover within 1 week to 6 months [S4][S5].
   - Damage to both anterior cingulates gives akinetic mutism: awake, eyes may follow, no speech or movement [S9].
   - Caudate lesions give abulia in 28% [S10].
   - Frontal eye field damage turns the eyes toward the lesion for days to about a week [S64].

5. Language and voice. The left hemisphere is dominant in about 95% of right-handers and 70% of left-handers [S14]; the game default is 90% of characters left-dominant [E]. Aphasia occurs in about 30% of ischaemic strokes [S13]. I defined ten vocal states from normal through slurred, non-fluent, jargon, moaning only and silent. Pain vocalisation survives aphasia [K].

6. Parietal. Neglect of one side occurs in 43% of acute right-hemisphere and 20% of left-hemisphere lesions, and in 17% vs 5% at 3 months [S17]. Anosognosia (unaware of the paralysis) occurs in 32% very acute, 18% in week 1 and 5% at 6 months [S19]. Pusher syndrome occurs in 10.4% overall, more often after right than left lesions [S20].

7. Occipital. Damage to both sides gives cortical blindness with normal pupil reactions, no blink to threat and no fixation [S22]. One side gives loss of half the visual field, with 2–10° of central vision often spared [S24].

8. Basal ganglia. A subthalamic lesion gives hemiballismus (violent flinging of one arm and leg) with EMG bursts of 200–1,000 ms, lasting weeks [S25][S26]. A putamen/capsule bleed gives hemiplegia with gaze toward the lesion [S27].

9. Thalamus. Eyes turn down and in with small pupils, sometimes the "wrong way" (away from the lesion) [S27][S29]. Thalamic astasia makes the character fall backward or to the opposite side with near-normal strength [S30]. Damage to both paramedian thalami gives coma or hypersomnolence with vertical gaze palsy [S28].

10. Cerebellum. The main findings:
   - Signs are on the same side as the lesion, with falls toward the lesion [S39][S41].
   - Nystagmus in 75% [S41], and 71% of cases with only vertigo cannot walk [S41].
   - Intention tremor below 5 Hz; Holmes tremor 2–4.5 Hz [S44].
   - Deterioration from swelling has a median of 3 days (10 h – 10 d) [S40].
   - The numeric gait values are author estimates [K/E].

11. Brainstem, partial lesions.
   - Third-nerve palsy: the eye turns 22–33° outward (up to 40°) and about 8° down, with a complete droop of the lid and a blown pupil [S50].
   - Sixth-nerve palsy (eye turned in) occurs in 1–2.7% of head injuries [S51].
   - INO, one-and-a-half syndrome and Millard-Gubler are covered [S52][S53][S62].
   - Ocular bobbing: fast downward jerk of 17.5° at 129°/s, then slow return, 2–15 times per minute [S54].
   - Wallenberg: vertigo, gait ataxia and Horner each 88%, nystagmus 71%, nausea/vomiting 65%, swallowing trouble 62%, hoarseness 41% [S58].
   - Massive pontine haemorrhage: death usually in 24–48 h [S57].

12. Eye-sign tables.
   - Gaze deviation toward a destroyed hemisphere [S63], away from a seizure focus in over 90% [S65], and away from a destroyed pons [K].
   - Ping-pong gaze has 1.5–8 s cycles [S67]; periodic alternating nystagmus reverses every 90–120 s [S46].
   - Pupils: 1–1.5 mm in pontine damage [S57], 5.0 ± 0.85 mm in brain death [S73], and a three-stage blown-pupil sequence in herniation [S74].
   - Fainting: unconscious 12.1 ± 4.4 s with eyes open and rolled up; 90% have irregular jerks [S70].

13. Rising pressure and herniation.
   - Midline shift vs consciousness: 0–3 mm alert, 3–4 mm drowsy, 6–8.5 mm stupor, 8–13 mm coma [S84].
   - The Cushing response appears when brain perfusion pressure falls below about 15 mmHg [S85].
   - Plateau waves: pressure rises to 50–100 mmHg for 5–20 minutes, with posturing [S86].
   - Central herniation is given as a stage table with pupils, breathing and posture [S87]. Stage durations are my estimates [E].

14. Epidural haematoma. A lucid interval occurs in 20–50% (the textbook form in under 20%) [S76]. Delayed cases appear from 2 h to 7 days, average 23 h [S77]. Treated mortality is 0–5% if not comatose and 11–41% if comatose [S78]. My default untreated EDH timeline gives about 40–90 minutes from first decline to death [E].

15. Subdural haematoma and outcome by pupils.
   - Subdural: 30% mortality with surgery within 4 h vs 90% after [S80].
   - Survival 46% with one fixed dilated pupil vs 13% with both [S89].
   - Mortality 16% / 38% / 59% with both, one or no pupils reacting [S92]; GCS 3 gives 51% mortality, and GCS-P 1 gives 74% [S92].
   - "Talk and die": 2.4–7.8% of head injuries; 25% of these had no haematoma [S82].

16. Seizures.
   - Immediate seizures (within 24 h) occur in 1–4% of brain injuries and early seizures (within 7 days) in 4–25% [S103].
   - Generalised seizures average 62 s [S104], and the jerks slow down before they stop [S105]. The figure-of-4 posture points to the seizure focus about 90% of the time [S106].
   - Frontal seizures last 10–40 s [S107].
   - Paralysis after a seizure lasts a mean of 173 s (11 s – 22 min) [S110]. Continuous focal jerking lasts over 1 h [S109].
   - Cerebellar and brainstem lesions do not cause epileptic seizures [K].

17. Posturing. I gave full joint-angle targets for decorticate, decerebrate, fencing and figure-of-4 postures [S111][E], plus a table to tell them apart. The fencing response appears in 66% of knockouts [S99].

18. GCS and the resolver. I gave the GCS eye/verbal/motor definitions [S93] and what each GCS band looks like.
   - The resolver formula combines destroyed tissue, concussive stun, ischaemia and compression into a severity per region, then maps it to body channels by side.
   - A fall-controller table covers each deficit type.
   - A region list with hit volumes is included [S38][K][E].

It covers what a real body does in the first 0–60 s after being shot, stabbed, punched, hammered or burned, and builds on round one without repeating it. Every section ends with a "Simulation parameters" table and a "Visual/behavioural checklist". The file also has a 25-row reaction-selection table, nine second-by-second test scenarios, a load-bearing list, a Suspicious content section and 65 references.

Research limits: about 60 web searches ran before the session's shared 200-call budget ran out; three planned searches were refused. WebFetch was not used. All sourced [S] values come from search summaries and abstracts, not full papers. Engine details are my own knowledge [K] and need checking.

Key findings:
1. **Startle / flinch [S1–S4]:** blink starts at 30 ms, neck at 62 ms, jaw at 67 ms, arms at 85–100 ms, legs at 100–140 ms. The whole-body flinch is complete within 200 ms of a pistol shot. It is biggest on the first shot and shrinks with repeats. There is no startle on an unconscious body.
2. **Withdrawal from pain or heat [S37]:** about 100 ms for a cut; 190–280 ms, then a second wave at 1.2–1.5 s, for heat. Pain behaviour is scaled down by arousal; the reflex is not [S6][S15][S17].
3. **Bullets never throw bodies [E]:** a 9 mm moves a 75 kg body 0.038 m/s and buckshot 0.17 m/s, against a backward step threshold of 0.13–0.22 m/s. A boxer's punch carries about 9× a 9 mm bullet's momentum and does push people back a step. Only the hit limb shows a small flick.
4. **Heart shot [S5][S13]:** about 10–15 s of full voluntary action. In witnessed suicides by a stab to the heart, 4 of 7 stayed active 2–10 min, 2 for about 10 s, and 1 dropped at once.
5. **Most stops are psychological [S5][S6][S8]:** handgun hits need about 2 hits on average to stop someone. The first 9 mm hit stops 47 %, and 13–17 % never stop. The game model sets stop probabilities per mindset (bystander, committed attacker, enraged, trained).
6. **People often miss the hit [S15][S16][S18]:** officers in shootings reported muted hearing (84 %), tunnel vision (79 %) and acting on autopilot (74 %). Only 32 % of badly wounded soldiers asked for painkillers, against 83 % of civilians. Stabs are often felt as punches. I added a "wound check" behaviour: look down, touch the wound, look at the hand for blood.
7. **Per-location mechanics [S46–S49]:** 21 regions are covered, with the fall probability for each. A broken thigh bone under load gives way in 0.1–0.3 s and the body falls toward that side. A mid-back spine hit drops the legs within 100 ms while the arms still work. 26.5 % of shot upper-arm fractures cause wrist drop.
8. **Balance and staggering [S19–S23]:** postural muscle response at 73–110 ms, recovery step at 0.24 s. One step can recover up to 32.2° of lean (23.5° for weaker people). Weak people take several steps, often crossing one foot over the other, and I gave a step-count model.
9. **Falls [S10][S24][S25][S51]:** seven fall types. Fall time is 0.6–1.2 s for a crumple and 1.0–1.6 s for a stiff topple, with the head hitting the ground at 2–7.4 m/s. Conscious people get their arms out by about 100 ms; hands land first in 74 % of real falls, but the head still hits in 37 %. Unconscious bodies show "no protective action / floppy".
10. **Faint or bleed-out collapse [S26][S27]:** unconscious for about 12 s, jerks in 90 %, eyes open and turned up. A bleed-out looks the same, but the victim does not wake.
11. **Knockouts [S28–S36]:** hooks average about 9,300 rad/s² of head rotation. Punches that knocked people out averaged 5,900 vs 3,500 rad/s² for those that did not; the proposed threshold is about 4,500. I give a knockout-probability formula based on this. Muscle tone goes within 100 ms. 53.9 % of MMA knockouts come from jaw strikes, and fighters take about 3.5 s of further blows while unconscious. "Rocked" is defined as staggering, stumbling and struggling to get up.
12. **Knife, burns, pain and neurological deficits [S38–S44]:** knife reactions (arm yanked back in 150–250 ms; defensive arms up). Flame contact gives withdrawal 0.2–0.6 s later. Pain face and scream acoustics are given as parameters (screams have a rough 30–150 Hz amplitude modulation). The doc spells out when people writhe and when they lie still. Brain-injury deficits change reactions: paralysed side, eyes crossing, twitching arms at 1–4 Hz, confusion slowing reactions ×1.3–3, loss of speech with swearing preserved.

I wrote the biomechanics document for the ragdoll and active-ragdoll system: 14 sections, each topic section ending in a "Simulation parameters" table and a "Visual/behavioural checklist".

Important limit: no new web research went into this document. The shared 200-search budget was already used up, and my first three searches (the de Leva table, the Dempster/Winter table, the trunk sub-segments) returned only a budget notice. WebFetch was not used, per the brief. So:
- The 20 [S#] tags reuse sources that the earlier round-two session (doc 02) had found; their URLs are in the references, and none was re-read here.
- Most numbers are [K], from named standard literature, or [E], with the arithmetic shown.
- The de Leva table was reproduced from memory and passes internal checks: masses sum to 100.0 %, and the trunk and head centre-of-mass (CM) and radii of gyration agree to under 0.1 mm between de Leva's two alternative endpoint definitions. It stays tagged (M) until someone opens the PDF.
- Section 12 lists what to verify first.

Key findings:
1. [Segments] Use de Leva, not Dempster. Dempster's elderly cadavers make the thigh 7.5 kg instead of 10.6 kg and the trunk 49.7 % instead of 43.5 %. The 75 kg table gives masses, CM positions and moments of inertia (MOI) about three axes for 11 segments, plus a head/neck split (4.4 / 0.8 kg) and female fractions [S1] (M).
2. [Whole body] Standing CM is 0.96 m. Pitch MOI is 11.8 kg·m² about the CM and 69.5 about the ankles, so the topple rate is 3.0 s⁻¹. Twist MOI is about 1.1 kg·m². Chain inertias: leg about the hip 2.67, arm about the shoulder 0.45, shank+foot 0.41, forearm+hand 0.078, head+neck about C7 0.11 kg·m². Stance gravity loads per side: ankle 318, knee 179, hip 79 Nm/rad [E].
3. [Ranges of motion] Four limits per joint: active, passive, limp/dead, and failure. Section 8.2 turns these into rig limits for a 3-body spine plus neck and head. Section 2.5 adds two-joint rules (a hamstring coupling torque; a tenodesis rule for limp hands), and section 2.6 gives the angles limp bodies settle at (feet splayed 30–60°, prone head turned 60–90°, ankles plantarflexed 40–60°) [K] (M).

Proposed rule [K](L): the arm extends on the side the face is turned to (asymmetric tonic neck reflex pattern), otherwise random. The 2-10 s duration is an engineering estimate [E]; the source only says 'seconds'.

corrections.claim: Decorticate posture (lesion above red nucleus): arms adducted, flexed at elbow/wrist/fingers, legs extended; decerebrate (midbrain/upper pons): arms extended, adducted, internally rotated and pronated, wrists/fingers flexed, legs extended and plantar-flexed.
corrections.correct_value: The descriptions and textbook lesion levels are correct. Nuances added: in humans the red-nucleus level rule is loose, both postures can coexist or alternate, and lesions below the vestibular nuclei give flaccidity. One error was fixed in the §18.5 checklist: 'backs of the hands turn out' now reads 'palms turn outward and backward', since internal rotation plus pronation turns the palm away from the body.

corrections.claim: Acoustic startle EMG onsets: orbicularis oculi 20-50 ms (pooled 30 +/- 1), masseter/SCM 55-85 ms (67 +/- 2, 62 +/- 13), biceps 85-100, hamstrings/quadriceps 100-125, tibialis anterior 130-140 ms; whole-body flinch within 200 ms of a pistol shot; largest on the first trial, then habituates
corrections.correct_value: Ranges and head-to-foot order stand. Jitter within the ranges, not by the pooled +/- values. Masseter and SCM can be treated as simultaneous (60-70 ms). Component onsets fall within about 200 ms; the whole pattern is over in about 0.5 s. The blink habituates least.
corrections.evidence: From memory of the classic human startle EMG papers (Wilkins et al., Brain 1986; Brown et al., Brain 1991) [K](H). The first-trial effect is Oude Nijhuis et al., J Neurophysiol 2010 [K]. I could not re-check the LASR 2026 pooled means (30+/-1, 67+/-2, 62+/-13). Their mixed spreads suggest the paper combines SE and SD. No web access in this pass: search budget exhausted, WebFetch blocked.

corrections.claim: Nociceptive withdrawal reflex (RIII) about 100 ms; radiant-heat withdrawal EMG about 190-280 ms (A-delta) and 1,170-1,460 ms (C-fibre)
corrections.correct_value: RIII about 90-100 ms onset in a 90-180 ms window is correct (leg; arm is 10-30 ms shorter). The heat values come from lower-limb stimulation in spinal-cord-injured subjects. Scale the C-fibre component by path length: hand 0.6-1.0 s, face 0.2-0.5 s. Aδ at the hand is about 150-250 ms.
corrections.evidence: RIII is Willer 1977 (sural nerve to biceps femoris) [K](H). The SCI heat numbers could not be re-verified. The two-component pattern and C-fibre conduction of about 1 m/s are standard physiology [K]. The document applied leg latencies to hand and face burns; this is now corrected in section 1.2 and the section 8 parameters.

corrections.claim: Bullet momentum negligible (9 mm 0.038 m/s, 00 buck 0.17 m/s on 75 kg) vs XcoM backward-step threshold 0.13-0.22 m/s; boxer's punch about 26.5 kg m/s, about 9x a 9 mm
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged. 9 mm: 8 g x 360 m/s = 2.88 kg m/s, which is 0.038 m/s on 75 kg. 00 buck: 31.5 g x 400 m/s = 12.6 kg m/s, which is 0.168 m/s. Backward threshold: 0.04-0.07 m x 3.20 = 0.13-0.22 m/s. Punch: 2.9 x 9.14 = 26.5 kg m/s = 9.2x.
corrections.evidence: All table entries recomputed. The punch value cross-checks against Walilko's peak force: 3,427 N as a 12 ms half-sine gives about 26 N s. The backward margin matches clinical limits of stability (about 4 deg backward at 0.96 m = 0.067 m) [K]. The bullets-knock-people-back myth is correctly rejected.

corrections.claim: Even if the heart is instantly destroyed there is sufficient oxygen in the brain for full voluntary action for 10-15 s; psychological incapacitation can never be counted on
corrections.correct_value: 10-15 s is the upper bound of the voluntary window. Loss of consciousness usually comes 6-12 s after cerebral flow stops, with degradation in the last 2-5 s.
corrections.evidence: The quotation and the psychological-factor list (including 'preconceived notions of what people do when shot') are the widely reproduced text of Patrick, FBI 1989 [K](H). The exact 'never be counted on' wording was not re-checked. The 6-12 s nuance comes from neck-cuff and induced-VF data [K].

corrections.claim: FBI 2014: those who stop after torso hits commonly do so because they decide to; pain often delayed by fight-or-flight; police hit rate 20-30 %
corrections.correct_value: The substance stands (psychological stops dominate; pain is often delayed). Attribute it to the FBI 1989/2014 position rather than as a verbatim quote until re-checked. The NYPD 18 % gunfight hit rate (RAND 2008) and Dallas about 35 % are consistent.
corrections.evidence: The 2014 memo's wording could not be re-verified without web access. The meaning matches the verified 1989 FBI conclusion [K].

corrections.claim: Ellifritz: about 2 handgun hits to stop (1.5-2.4 across calibres); 9 mm 47 % stopped by first torso/head hit, 34 % one-shot stop; 13-17 % never incapacitated (.38/9mm/.40/.45); shotgun 86 % one-hit, 12 % never

corrections.claim: Karger 1999 witnessed cardiac-stab suicides: 4/7 active 2-10 min, 2/7 about 10 s, 1/7 immediate; ulnar artery, great saphenous vein and peripheral lung/liver wounds allowed hours of activity
corrections.correct_value: Keep, but only as a small-sample (n=7) shape, not as probabilities.
corrections.evidence: The paper is real (Karger, Niemeyer, Brinkmann, Int J Legal Med 1999;112:188-191) and its general finding matches round one [R1-03 section 5]. The 4/2/1 breakdown and the hours figure could not be re-verified (PubMed fetch blocked). The hours are physiologically plausible for those vessels [K].

corrections.claim: Fall from standing 2/3 s to >= 1 s after a tone-abolishing hit; unavoidable falls 700-1,200 ms; protective arm EMG about 100 ms; early arm reactions in 91 % of young adults' falls
corrections.correct_value: Keep. Timings are physically consistent: COM free fall from 0.96 m to about 0.2 m takes 0.39 s (lower bound), and knee folding or toppling gives 0.6-1.2 s. An arm burst at about 100 ms is consistent. The 91 % is unverified.
corrections.evidence: Physics recomputed [E]. Upper-limb balance reactions at about 80-140 ms and about 0.7 s to impact in lateral falls are known [K]. The Force Science 2010 and J Biomech 2023 figures were not re-checked.

corrections.claim: 227 videotaped real falls: hand impact 74 %, head impact 37 %, hand impact did not reduce head impact; causes weight shift 41 %, trip 21 %, hit/bump 11 %, loss of support 11 %, collapse 11 % (all attributed to Robinovitch, Lancet 2013)
corrections.correct_value: Numbers correct. Hand 74 % / head 37 % / no protective effect of the hands belong to Schonnop et al., CMAJ 2013;185:E803-E810 (same SFU video dataset, 227 falls by 133 residents; head impact more likely in forward falls). The causes belong to Robinovitch et al., Lancet 2013 (227 falls by 130 residents). Added as [S24b].
corrections.evidence: From the checker's knowledge of both papers [K](M-H). Fixed in section 5.3, the parameters, section 14 row 6, section 15 item 12 and the references. The same misattribution appears in research2/03_falling_ragdoll_biomechanics.md (not edited; out of scope).

corrections.claim: Standing-fall head impact velocity 95 % PI 2.02-7.41 m/s; rigid topple 1.0-1.6 s with about 6.5-7 m/s head impact
corrections.correct_value: Topple arithmetic confirmed: 1.00/1.25/1.57 s from 10/5/2 deg, crown 7.2 m/s, head centre about 6.5 m/s. Use 0.8-1.6 s when knees and ankles are not fully locked. The 2.02-7.41 m/s interval is unverified, but its upper end matches the physical ceiling sqrt(3gL) = 7.2 m/s.
corrections.evidence: Re-derived: cosh phase 0.59/0.84/1.16 s plus energy phase (1/omega) ln[tan(pi/8)/tan(0.125)] = 0.41 s. A non-uniform human body (I_feet/m about 1.08 m^2) changes omega by only about 2 %. The Hajiaghamemar et al. 2015 paper is real [K], but the interval was not re-checked.

corrections.claim: Postural response EMG 73-110 ms; recovery-step toe-off 0.24 +/- 0.03 s; single-step lean limit 32.2 deg young vs 23.5 deg older; weaker people take multiple steps, about half crossover
corrections.correct_value: EMG 73-110 ms and lean limits of about 32 deg / about 23-24 deg are confirmed (M). Toe-off widened to 0.22-0.35 s (0.24 s is the fast end). The 50 % crossover is unverified.
corrections.evidence: Horak & Nashner 1986 distal-to-proximal ankle strategy [K](M). Thelen et al. 1997, same paradigm, gave about 32.5 deg vs 23.9 deg [K](M). Typical compensatory-step foot-off is about 0.25-0.35 s [K]. Crossover and multi-step patterns in weaker people are consistent with Maki & McIlroy [K].

corrections.claim: Complete syncope: loss of consciousness 12.1 +/- 4.4 s, myoclonic jerks 90 %, eyes open, early upward deviation (13/14, some starting with downbeat nystagmus)
corrections.correct_value: 12.1 +/- 4.4 s, 90 % myoclonus, 79 % other movements, eyes open with early upgaze. The 7/6/1 of 14 eye counts are unverified. The upgaze is transient; the dead rest near neutral or slightly divergent, never 'rolled back'.
corrections.evidence: Lempert, Bauer & Schmidt, Ann Neurol 1994 (59 volunteers, 56 episodes, 42 complete syncopes) [K](H). The eyes-at-death myth note was added in line with R1-04 sections 11 and 14.

corrections.claim: Knockout biomechanics: hook 9,306 +/- 4,485 rad/s^2, 71 g; LOC punches 5.9 +/- 2.4 vs 3.5 +/- 1.6 krad/s^2; concussion threshold about 4,500 rad/s^2, DAI/ASDH about 10,000; immediate tone loss within about 100 ms
corrections.correct_value: Walilko straight punch (9.14 m/s, 3,427 N, 2.9 kg, 58 g, 6,343 rad/s^2) and the Viano hook (11.0 m/s, 71.2 g, 9,306 rad/s^2) are confirmed. 4,500 rad/s^2 is the 25 %-risk concussion level (Zhang 2004: 4,600/5,900/7,900 for 25/50/80 %), not a loss-of-consciousness threshold. About 10,000 rad/s^2 matches bridging-vein (ASDH) tolerance for pulses under 10 ms (Depreitere 2006). The P_LOC midpoint should shift to 7,500-8,000 for braced or aware targets. The 5.9/3.5 krad/s^2 values and the <=100 ms figure are unverified (video shows tone lost within 0.1-0.2 s).
corrections.evidence: From the checker's knowledge [K](M-H). The logistic arithmetic was re-checked: 0.11/0.22/0.50/0.94 at 3,500/4,500/6,000/9,300. The KO-eyes mechanism was also corrected: tonic upgaze of loss of consciousness, not Bell's phenomenon.

corrections.claim: MMA: 53.9 % of knockout strikes to the jaw region; mean 3.5 s (0-20 s) from KO strike to stoppage
corrections.correct_value: 53.9 % and 3.5 s (0-20 s). About 2.6 further strikes land in that interval ([K], L-M). The 'n = 503 UFC matches' stated elsewhere is doubtful; the paper is usually cited as 844 fights.
corrections.evidence: Hutchison, Lawrence, Cusimano & Schweizer, Am J Sports Med 2014 [K](M). Not re-checked on the web.

corrections.claim: Consensus video signs include 'no protective action - floppy' and 'motor incoordination'; slow to get up is the most sensitive NFL sign (66 %)
corrections.correct_value: The six Davis 2019 signs and the motor-incoordination definition are confirmed. 'Slow to get up' is an NFL-specific extra sign, and its 66 % is unverified. These are P(sign | concussion), not P(sign | hit).
corrections.evidence: Davis et al., BJSM 2019 [K](H). The NFL 2020 figures were not re-checked.

corrections.claim: 157 officers: diminished sound 84 %, tunnel vision 79 %, automatic pilot 74 %, slow motion 62 %; Anzio: 32 % of severely wounded soldiers vs 83 % of civilians wanted narcotics

It shows the effect of context on pain, not in-fight analgesia.
corrections.evidence: Artwohl & Christensen, Deadly Force Encounters 1997 [K](H). Beecher 1946 and 1956 [K](M).

corrections.correct_value: Use 0.2-0.3 for ballistic radial palsy (30/113 = 26.5 % checks arithmetically). Thoracic predominance is plausible. Inability to bear weight after hip GSW is correct.

corrections.claim: ISO 13732-1 uses 0.5 s as the minimum contact period for unintentional touching; real contact with hot metal above 70 C typically lasts 1-5 s; heat pain threshold about 43-45 C
corrections.correct_value: The 43-45 C pain threshold and 44 C burn onset are confirmed. 0.5 s is only the shortest period ISO 13732-1 tabulates; design practice (IEC Guide 117, EN 563) uses 1 s for an alert adult's unintentional touch and 4 s for slowed reactions, so use 0.5-1 s and 4 s. '1-5 s real contact' is probably a misreading of those 1 s / 4 s design periods; it is re-tagged [E] and kept only for gripping or pinned contact. Added bare-metal burn thresholds: about 65-70 C at 1 s, 58-60 C at 4 s, 55 C at 10 s, 51 C at 1 min, 48 C at 10 min, 43 C at 8 h.
corrections.evidence: From the checker's knowledge of ISO 13732-1, IEC Guide 117 and Moritz & Henriques 1947 [K](M). The In Compliance article could not be re-read.

corrections.correct_value: The first-blow rule is confirmed, with an exception added for a head that is already bleeding. The per-blow increments remain unverified [E].
corrections.evidence: The BPA first-blow rule (blood must be exposed before it can be spattered or cast off) is standard teaching. Forensic hammer series describe the qualitative sequence, but no per-blow increments were available to check.

corrections.claim: Tibia commonest open fracture (anteromedial cover 3-8 mm); protruding bone ends slip back when the limb straightens; direct blow gives transverse/butterfly, torsion gives spiral (2-4x shaft diameter), high energy gives comminuted
corrections.correct_value: All confirmed. Spiral length is consistent with geometry: a 45 deg helix gives 1.6-3.1x diameter for 180-360 deg of wrap. Cover can exceed 10 mm in obese legs.
corrections.evidence: Standard orthopaedic trauma teaching (Gustilo-Anderson; Rockwood & Green), reviewer knowledge. Helix calc: axial advance per turn = pi x diameter.

corrections.claim: Flail chest = 3 or more adjacent ribs each broken in 2+ places (ATLS); paradox 0.5-1 cm quiet, 1-3 cm laboured, up to 5 cm; rib fractures start at ~20% compression, flail at 35-40%
corrections.correct_value: ATLS 10th ed. defines flail as >=2 adjacent ribs each fractured in >=2 places; >=3 is the other common definition. Game rule: >=2, with half the paradox for 2-rib segments. Compression thresholds confirmed (first fracture ~20-25%, flail ~40%). Excursion values stay [E]; the force arithmetic is correct.
corrections.evidence: Reviewer recall of ATLS 10th-edition wording. Kroell regression AIS = -3.78 + 19.56*C gives AIS1 at C~0.24, AIS3 at ~0.35, AIS4 (flail) at ~0.40. Calc: 0.015 m2 x 490-3,920 Pa = 7-59 N.

corrections.claim: LV wounds jet scarlet in systole only (20-60 cm); RV and atrial wounds well dark blood; small oblique LV stabs self-seal causing tamponade; stab chamber split RV ~40%, LV ~35%, RA ~15%, LA ~5%
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed. Fixed an internal inconsistency: sim weights had 'multiple 0.05' while §10.1 says 20-30% multi-chamber. Now: first chamber RV 0.42 / LV 0.37 / RA 0.16 / LA 0.05, then a second-chamber roll with p = 0.2-0.3.
corrections.evidence: Physiology: LV diastolic pressure is 5-12 mmHg with the aortic valve closed. Jet height is bounded by P/(rho*g) ~1.5 m at 120 mmHg. Penetrating-cardiac series rank RV > LV > RA > LA (reviewer knowledge).

corrections.claim: Fatal tamponade leaves 150-450 mL at autopsy vs 100-200 mL clinical; sac distended and blue-purple; neck veins distended
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed; upper bound widened to 500 mL (typical 250-350). Caveat added: low-pressure tamponade in hypovolaemia gives flat neck veins, and neck-vein distension is not a usable sign at autopsy.
corrections.evidence: Consistent with round one's verified clinical 100-200 mL (R1-03 V7, V8) and its low-pressure tamponade note (V7). The distended, bluish sac is the standard forensic description.

corrections.claim: Open (sucking) pneumothorax when chest-wall defect >= 2/3 tracheal diameter (~10-13 mm); handgun entrances 4-6 mm are below this
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed as the ATLS rule of thumb, not a sharp physical threshold; smaller straight tracks can still admit some air.
corrections.evidence: ATLS teaching (reviewer knowledge). 9 mm entrance of 4-6 mm matches R1-01 §2.

corrections.claim: AAST 2018 grades for liver, spleen and kidney as tabulated; liver/spleen/kidney/brain inelastic and burst into stellate fissures under rifle cavitation, lung and muscle elastic
corrections.correct_value: Tables match in substance. Added: liver grade I capsular tear; advance one grade for multiple (or bilateral kidney) injuries up to grade III; vascular injury = pseudoaneurysm or AV fistula. Fissure lengths 3-10+ cm remain [E]. Added an explicit warning against remote 'hydrostatic shock'.
corrections.evidence: Reviewer independent recall of Kozar et al., J Trauma Acute Care Surg 2018;85:1119-1122, and of Fackler's elastic/inelastic grouping (JAMA 1988). Not checked against the documents themselves.

corrections.claim: A cut through the windpipe at or below the vocal cords removes the voice; air bubbles through blood on exhalation; aspirated blood coughed out as spray from the neck wound
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed. Caveat: a weak voice can return if neck flexion or clot closes the wound, so voice_state should follow wound gape.
corrections.evidence: Phonation requires expired air to pass the vocal folds; an open airway below them diverts it, as with an uncapped tracheostomy. Standard forensic cut-throat descriptions.

corrections.claim: Knife cannot cut the cervical spine except through a disc space (30-80 strokes, 30-120 s); severed head LOC ~2-10 s; facial/jaw movements 10-30 s; body limp
corrections.correct_value: Principle confirmed. Severed-head LOC 4-10 s, default 7 (was 2-10, default 6). Knife duration widened to 30-180 s. The unsupported 'pupils constrict briefly' was removed, and a myth note added that eyes do not 'roll back' at death.
corrections.evidence: Rossen, Kabat & Anderson 1943: LOC 5-10 s, mean 6.8 s after complete arrest of cerebral flow (verified in R2-04 and R1-03). van Rijn 2011 in rats: ~4 s, a lower bound because rat cerebral metabolism is faster. The 2 s floor was below both.

corrections.claim: Cast-off drop volume ~50 uL x g/a: hammer (~17 g) ~3 uL, knife (~9 g) ~5 uL, 2-8 mm stains; minimum blows ~ cast-off trails + 1
corrections.correct_value: Arithmetic and rule confirmed. Clarified that the rule gives a minimum (+2 if the final blow had no backswing).
corrections.evidence: Calc: 10^2/0.6 = 167 m/s2 = 17 g -> 2.9 uL (1.8 mm drop); 8^2/0.7 = 91 m/s2 = 9.3 g -> 5.4 uL (2.2 mm). Trails+1 is standard BPA teaching (Bevel & Gardner; James, Kish & Sutton), reviewer knowledge.

corrections.claim: Arterial projected pattern: 8-25 mL per heartbeat from carotid or femoral wound, one cluster per beat along arcs/zigzags, lower and smaller as BP falls; stains over ~4-5 mm run on vertical walls
corrections.correct_value: Per-beat 6-25 mL (initial value, falls quickly); the pattern description is confirmed. Correction: the 4-5 mm run threshold is a drop diameter (~30-60 uL, leaving ~10-20 mm wall stains), not a stain diameter. 4-5 mm stains do not run.
corrections.evidence: Round one gives carotid 1,000-2,500 and femoral 800-2,000 mL/min, i.e. 800/140 to 2,500/100 = 6-25 mL per beat. A 4 mm drop is 34 uL and a 5 mm drop 65 uL.

corrections.claim: Pool timeline: gels in 3-15 min; clot shrinks to ~50% volume in 1-2 h; 2-20 mm straw-yellow serum ring at 30 min-3 h; cracked crust after 12-72 h
corrections.correct_value: Plausible and consistent with round one. Keep the default gel time at 5-15 min (Lee-White) and use 3 min only for thin films.
corrections.evidence: R1-03 verified Lee-White 5-15 min [V13]; serum separation from 30-60 min; drying 24-72 h. Clinical clot-retraction test: starts at ~30-60 min, about half the volume expressed by 1-2 h.

corrections.claim: Drip-trail spacing = walking speed / drip rate; stain W/L = sin(atan(sqrt(2gh)/v)): walking 0.94-0.96, running 4 m/s 0.70-0.74; footprints fade to 0.60-0.75 per step, visible 5-15 steps
corrections.correct_value: Kinematics and W/L values confirmed. Footprint decay corrected to 0.60-0.80 per step (6-13 visible steps); 0.60-0.75 only gives 6-10 steps to 5% intensity. Caveat added: drops from a swinging hand take the hand's speed (~0-3 m/s), so W/L can fall to ~0.8.

corrections.claim: Exposed muscle turns brighter red in air within 10-30 min (oxymyoglobin bloom) and brown after death over 2-6 h; gape 0.5-1.0x depth across fibres, 0.1-0.2x along
corrections.correct_value: Bloom chemistry confirmed, but it applies mainly to non-perfused (dead) tissue: use a weak bloom (<=30-50% of the lerp) in living wounds and the full bloom over 15-30 min after death. Post-mortem browning in 2-6 h is plausible but driven mostly by drying. Gape direction is correct; the numbers remain [E].
corrections.evidence: Meat-science colour chemistry (Mancini & Hunt) describes post-mortem tissue. Living muscle is perfused and blood-covered, and mitochondrial O2 use at 37 C keeps the bloom layer thin. No data were available on gape ratios.

The Fact-check section is §21 of the file, with per-claim verdicts, other corrections, a myth table and open gaps. §18 has a pointer to it, §19 was updated, and references 24-29 were added (from memory, not opened).

corrections.claim: Impact spectrum is flat to ~1/τc, with its first zero at 1.5/τc; τc = π√(m/k)
corrections.correct_value: A half-sine force pulse stays within 3 dB up to about 0.6/τc and is about −9.5 dB at 1/τc. Its first true zero is at 1.5/τc and the envelope falls at 12 dB/oct above that. τc = π√(m/k) is correct; use the reduced mass for two moving bodies. The impact_band_limit LP corner moves from 1.5/τc to about 0.6/τc.
corrections.evidence: Re-derived: |F(f)| ∝ |cos(πfτ)/(1−4f²τ²)|. The apparent zero at fτ = 0.5 cancels (π/4, −2.1 dB). At fτ = 1 the value is 1/3 (−9.5 dB), and at fτ = 0.6 it is 0.70 (−3.1 dB). No web access: the search budget was used up and WebFetch was EGRESS_BLOCKED.

corrections.claim: Fist-to-face contact ≈12 ms (so force content < ~125 Hz), from Walilko 2005 (effective mass 2.9 kg, 9.1 m/s, ~3.4 kN), labelled 'bare fist'
corrections.correct_value: About 12 ms for gloved Olympic-boxer punches to a Hybrid III dummy face: π×26.5/(2×3,427) = 12.1 ms, first zero about 125 Hz. A bare-knuckle punch is estimated at about 5–10 ms [E], first zero about 150–300 Hz. punch_contact_time was split into gloved and bare values.
corrections.evidence: The arithmetic checks out and matches the R2-02 cross-check (impulse (2/π)·3,427·0.012 ≈ 26 N·s). That Walilko's boxers wore competition gloves is my own recall (medium confidence); the paper was not reachable.

corrections.claim: Head-on-concrete 2–8 ms, trunk-on-floor 20–80 ms, steel-on-bone 0.2–1 ms
corrections.correct_value: Head 2–8 ms and trunk 20–80 ms are confirmed. Steel on bone is 0.2–0.5 ms only on bare bone or teeth; through 2–5 mm of skin it is about 0.7–2 ms (k ≈ 10⁶–10⁷ N/m for a 0.5 kg hammer head).

corrections.claim: Soft tissue has no audible resonance; living skull first resonance ~0.8–1.5 kHz, damping 3–10 %, so bone rings only 3–20 ms
corrections.correct_value: Soft tissue does not ring (confirmed). A skull mode near 1 kHz with ζ 0.03–0.10 matches my recall of Håkansson 1994. With the doc's own parameters, though, τ = 1/(2πfζ) ≈ 1–7 ms and T60 ≈ 7–45 ms, so the audible ring is about 10–40 ms, not 3–20 ms.
corrections.evidence: Arithmetic: 0.8 kHz at ζ 0.03 gives τ 6.6 ms (T60 46 ms); 1.5 kHz at ζ 0.10 gives τ 1.06 ms (T60 7.3 ms). Håkansson was not re-opened.

corrections.claim: Bullet-impact sound reaches the shooter d/v_bullet + d/343 s after the shot (≈115 ms at 20 m, handgun)
corrections.correct_value: t = d/v + d/c; 20 m handgun = 57.1 + 58.3 = 115 ms. All 8 table cells re-derived correctly. Bullet deceleration is ignored, which adds a few percent for rifles at 100 m. Separately, the checklist line 'about a tenth of a second at 30 m' was corrected to 0.12 s (rifle) to 0.17 s (handgun).

corrections.claim: Muzzle blast is 60–90 dB louder than the bullet impact
corrections.correct_value: Plausible as an order of magnitude. At equal 1 m distance the doc's own levels (150–165 vs 75–95 dB) give 55–90 dB; at the shooter with the target 20 m away the gap is about 80–115 dB. The impact level is itself an [E] (L) estimate.
corrections.evidence: dB arithmetic from the doc's own values. No calibrated impact recordings exist to check against.

corrections.claim: Blood jets exit at ≤5.5 m/s (3.3–4.4 typical) and make no orifice noise; arterial bleeding is heard only where the jet lands
corrections.correct_value: ≤5.5 m/s at 120 mmHg is confirmed. The upper bound rises to about 5.9–6.7 m/s at systolic 140–180 mmHg, which is common in a frightened, injured person. 3.3–4.4 m/s is itself an estimate (Cv 0.6–0.8). No orifice noise; the exception is blood driven out with air (open airway, sucking wound, jugular air entry).
corrections.evidence: Bernoulli: √(2·15,996/1,060) = 5.49; √(2·23,998/1,060) = 6.73 m/s. Consistent with R1-06 §8.1 and R1-03 §6.2 (no measured human jet speeds exist).

corrections.claim: Bubble 'plink' frequency in blood ≈ 3.2 / bubble radius (m); floor pools (~2.5 mm) are too shallow for a ringing bubble, so drips 'pat' not 'plink'
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed: f0 = 3.19/a for blood (water 3.28/a). The maximum puddle height of 2√(σ/ρg)·sin(θ/2) ≈ 2.3–3.3 mm matches 2.5 mm, and the crater of a 4–5 mm drop bottoms out on the floor. Separate fix: the bubble ring time was too long. τ = Q/(πf0) with Q ≈ 15–35 gives about 1 ms (0.5 mm), 2–3 ms (1 mm), 4–7 ms (2 mm) and 15–20 ms (5 mm); the doc had 3–15 ms for 0.5–2 mm.
corrections.evidence: Minnaert arithmetic with γ 1.4, p0 101,325 Pa, ρ 1,060 kg/m³. Capillary length √(0.055/(1,060·9.81)) = 2.3 mm. Bubble damping δ ≈ 0.03–0.06 is my own knowledge (medium confidence).

corrections.claim: Breath-sound power rises ~flow^1.75–2; tracheal breath sound 100–1,500 Hz
corrections.correct_value: The exponent and band are consistent with my recall of Gavriely & Cugell and Pasterkamp. However, the doc's gloss '+10–12 dB per doubling of flow' was wrong: power ∝ flow^n gives 3.0·n dB per doubling, i.e. +5.3–6.0 dB. This is corrected in §5.1, §17 and the parameter table.
corrections.evidence: Arithmetic: 10·1.75·log10(2) = 5.3 dB and 10·2·log10(2) = 6.0 dB; +10–12 dB would need n ≈ 3.5–4. The §5.3 recipe (amplitude ∝ flow) was already consistent.

corrections.claim: CORSA: crackles <20 ms (fine 2CD <10 ms, coarse >10 ms); wheeze ≥100 ms and >100 Hz; stridor loud, high-pitched, inspiratory with upper-airway narrowing
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed. Stridor is inspiratory for extrathoracic narrowing, expiratory for intrathoracic tracheal narrowing, and biphasic when fixed or severe. A stridor default of 500–800 Hz was added, since many descriptions put it above about 500 Hz.
corrections.evidence: My own knowledge of Sovijärvi et al. 2000 (high confidence); not re-opened.

corrections.claim: Sucking chest wound: small/slit holes pass air at ~20–50 m/s and hiss or whistle (f ≈ 0.2·v/d); large holes (≳10–15 mm) pass ~5–10 m/s and slurp/bubble
corrections.correct_value: For small holes, 20–50 m/s needs a pressure difference of about 2–15 cmH2O. The −10 to −40 cmH2O the doc quoted would give 40–80 m/s, an internal inconsistency. Large holes run about 1–9 m/s, falling with size (12 mm: 4–9, 15 mm: 3–6, 25 mm: 1–2 m/s at 0.5–1 L/s). The whistle estimate f ≈ 0.2·v/d is confirmed (1.2 kHz at 30 m/s through 5 mm). The two-thirds-of-tracheal-diameter threshold is standard ATLS teaching.
corrections.evidence: Bernoulli v = √(2ΔP/ρ_air): 2 cmH2O = 18 m/s, 15 = 50, 40 = 81 m/s. Continuity Q/A for the large holes.

corrections.claim: Open airway in the neck: 0.5–2 L/s through 1–5 cm² gives 2–30 m/s (§5.5, neck_airway_v)
corrections.correct_value: 1–20 m/s. A wide, gaping cut throat mostly bubbles and sucks; a narrow tracheal stab hisses.
corrections.evidence: Continuity: 0.5 L/s ÷ 5 cm² = 1 m/s; 2 L/s ÷ 1 cm² = 20 m/s.

corrections.claim: A tracheal wound below the vocal cords makes the victim aphonic
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed for an open, gaping wound: air leaves before the glottis, as with an uncapped tracheostomy. Nuance added: a small or partly closed hole leaves a weak, breathy voice and crackling surgical emphysema; occluding the hole restores a weak voice.
corrections.evidence: Standard physiology (my own knowledge, high confidence); consistent with R2-05 §14.2.

corrections.claim: Aspiration of blood caused 36.5 % of deaths in a 74-case cut-throat autopsy series
corrections.correct_value: Arithmetic is consistent (27/74 = 36.5 %, 37/74 = 50 % exsanguination). The paper was not re-verified. It is a fatal series, so it over-represents deep airway cuts.
corrections.evidence: [S8] was unreachable (no web). The R1-02 and R2-04 fact-checks reached the same 'not re-verified, arithmetic consistent' verdict.

corrections.claim: Screams are characterised by roughness (amplitude modulation 30–150 Hz)
corrections.correct_value: 30–150 Hz roughness (Arnal et al. 2015), versus about 4–5 Hz syllabic modulation in speech.
corrections.evidence: My own knowledge (high confidence); also verified in the R2-02 fact-check.

corrections.claim: Pain-vocalisation F0, F0 range, loudness and nonlinear phenomena rise with pain intensity; individual voice pitch is preserved from speech to screams and pain cries
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed, with a caveat added: Raine et al. (Bioacoustics) and Pisanski et al. (R Soc Open Sci 2020) used acted vocalisations. Pitch is preserved as a correlation across people, not as a fixed ratio for each person.
corrections.evidence: My own knowledge (medium confidence); the paper title states the preservation finding. The childbirth study is the only real-pain sample among the cited sources.

corrections.claim: Vocal SPL rises 8–9 dB per doubling of subglottal pressure; screaming needs ~30–60 cmH2O
corrections.correct_value: 8–9 dB per doubling of Ps (sound pressure ∝ Ps^~1.5) is confirmed. The phonation threshold of about 3 cmH2O and 5–10 cmH2O for conversation are standard. 30–60 cmH2O for screaming is plausible (loud singing reaches 40–60).
corrections.evidence: My own knowledge of Titze & Sundberg 1992 (medium-to-high confidence); not re-opened.

corrections.claim: ...so voice loudness must fall with shock (budget: class III ≤85–90 dB, class IV ≤65 dB at 1 m)
corrections.correct_value: Keep the caps as [E] game values, but the mechanism is wrong. Healthy maximal expiratory pressure is about 100–200+ cmH2O, so 30–60 cmH2O stays reachable. What removes loud screaming in shock is falling consciousness and drive, air hunger with short breath groups, and weakness from hypoperfusion. The caps should also be gated on consciousness and breath budget.
corrections.evidence: My own physiology knowledge (medium confidence). A mechanism note was added to §6.5 and §17.

corrections.claim: Average speech levels at 1 m: normal 62, raised 68, loud 75, shouted 82 dB SPL; maximal screams ~90–105 dB
corrections.correct_value: ANSI S3.5-1997 gives 62.35 / 68.34 / 74.85 / 82.30 dB SPL at 1 m. The scream range is plausible (maximal voice is usually measured at 30 cm; rare screamers exceed 110 dB at 1 m). Default 98 kept; up to 110 allowed for rare characters.
corrections.evidence: My own knowledge of the ANSI standard (high confidence); scream range low-to-medium confidence.

corrections.claim: Pain face = AU4 + max(AU6,AU7) + max(AU9,AU10) + AU43 (PSPI 0–16); pain closes the eyes whereas fear opens them (AU5)
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed. AU4, 6, 7, 9 and 10 are scored 0–5 and AU43 is binary, so the maximum is 16. Nuance: eyes are shut at the apex of each pain burst, not throughout.
corrections.evidence: My own knowledge of Prkachin & Solomon 2008 (high confidence); consistent with the R2-02 fact-check.

corrections.claim: Fear prototype AU1+2+4+5+7+20+26; surprise 1+2+5B+26; sadness 1+4+15; anger 4+5+7+23; disgust 9+15+16
corrections.correct_value: All match the FACS Investigator's Guide / EMFACS prototypes. Variants were noted in the rows (e.g. fear 1+2+4+5+20+25/26/27; disgust 10+15+16).
corrections.evidence: My own knowledge (high confidence).

corrections.claim: Central facial palsy weakens the contralateral lower face and largely spares the forehead and eye closure, and emotional smiling may be preserved; peripheral palsy paralyses the whole ipsilateral half-face with incomplete closure and Bell's phenomenon
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed. Gap added: the reverse dissociation ('emotional facial paresis': voluntary movement normal, emotional smiling weak) occurs with thalamic, striatocapsular, insular and medial frontal lesions. Bell's phenomenon is a normal reflex in about 75–90 % of people and is visible only when the lid fails to close.
corrections.evidence: My own knowledge (high confidence).

corrections.claim: Central cyanosis turns the tongue and oral mucosa blue; peripheral cyanosis leaves the tongue pink. Lip colour lags arterial saturation ~5–15 s, fingers ~15–30 s
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed. The finger lag can exceed 60 s under vasoconstriction or cold.
corrections.evidence: Cross-check with circulation times: arm-to-tongue about 10–16 s minus arm-to-lung about 4–8 s gives lung-to-tongue of about 5–10 s. Hamber 1999 is recalled, not re-opened.

corrections.claim: Apnoea at rest on room air: SpO2 stays >90 % for ~60–120 s, then falls steeply; struggling roughly halves this
corrections.correct_value: Plausible for an upright, calm adult. A supine, frightened or injured victim is probably about 45–90 s (FRC falls about 20 % supine and oxygen use rises); struggling gives about 30–60 s. The M28 citation (Benumof 1997) models pre-oxygenated patients (SaO2 90 % at about 8 min) and does not support the room-air figure.
corrections.evidence: Estimate from the room-air lung oxygen store: FRC about 2.5 L at about 14 % O2 ≈ 350 mL against about 250 mL/min consumption. My own knowledge of Benumof's curves. Not verified.

corrections.claim: Capillary refill ≤2 s is normal; >3 s indicates poor perfusion; no refill in the dead
corrections.correct_value: These are the conventional cut-offs. Upper normal limits vary: about 2 s in children and men, about 3 s in women, about 4.5 s in the elderly (Schriger & Baraff 1988, recalled); cold adds 1–2 s. The dead have no active refill; unfixed livor re-colours slowly and passively after pressure (tens of seconds to minutes).
corrections.evidence: My own knowledge (medium-to-high confidence).

corrections.claim: Broca aphasia ≈0.5–2 syllables/s (10–50 words/min) with 1–5 s pauses versus 4–6 syllables/s normally; Wernicke jargon is fluent with normal prosody; ataxic dysarthria is scanning with explosive loudness
corrections.correct_value: 10–50 words/min is about 0.25–1.2 syllables/s overall (1–3 syll/s within short runs), not 0.5–2. Normal 4–6 syll/s is the articulation rate; overall conversation (150–190 words/min) is about 3.5–4.5 syll/s. The Wernicke and ataxic descriptions are confirmed; the <50 words/min non-fluent boundary is classic.
corrections.evidence: Arithmetic at about 1.4 syllables per word; my own knowledge of the Darley/Aronson/Brown clusters and the classic aphasia criteria.

corrections.claim: The face does not keep its last expression after death; tone loss plus gravity shape it (supine jaw open 10–30 mm, cheeks shift 3–10 mm); cadaveric spasm is rare and affects the hands
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed. Nuances: a brief tonic anoxic grimace can follow LOC and relaxes within about a minute. Cadaveric spasm is mostly the hands, occasionally a limb, and is disputed as an entity separate from early rigor. Sag magnitudes remain [E].
corrections.evidence: Forensic knowledge (my own, medium-to-high confidence); consistent with R2-04 and R1-04.

corrections.claim: Saccade duration ≈ 21 ms + 2.2 ms per degree; basal tear secretion 1–2 µL/min; conjunctival sac overflows beyond ~25–30 µL
corrections.correct_value: D = 2.2·A + 21 ms is the standard main-sequence fit for about 1–40°. Basal tear flow is about 1.2 µL/min (Mishima, recalled). Resident tear volume is about 7 µL and the sac capacity about 25–30 µL.
corrections.evidence: My own knowledge (high confidence for the saccades, medium-to-high for the tears); not re-opened.

corrections.claim: §2.2 'Victim's forced grunt' caused by chest compression when shot
corrections.correct_value: This is an optional startle or pain vocalisation, often absent. A 9 mm bullet carries about 2.9 N·s, which moves a 75 kg body about 0.04 m/s and cannot compress the chest (a myth-adjacent error: bullet push). The chest 'huff' applies only to blunt blows and falls.
corrections.evidence: Momentum arithmetic, consistent with the R2-02 §1.3 fact-check.

corrections.claim: §6.3 P(vocalise) per pain spike applied at the moment of injury (implicit 'everyone screams when shot')
corrections.correct_value: An awareness gate was added: ×0 while unaware of the hit (P(unaware) 0.3–0.5 for gunshots under high arousal, 0.3–0.6 for torso stabs), with the pain spike applied when the wound is discovered. Silence, a grunt or 'I'm hit' are common.
corrections.evidence: Consistent with R2-02 §2.4 and §14 row 15, which is sourced from officer-involved-shooting and survivor literature.
